Our findings indicate that loss function performance varies significantly across different datasets and scenarios. In some cases, alternative loss functions outperformed the cross-entropy method, but in other instances, it failed to do so. Our results also show that loss function performance is not directly correlated with how well the models generalize to new data. We believe our findings offer valuable insights for researchers and practitioners when selecting loss functions for classification tasks. Furthermore, we propose several novel loss functions that could be used in future research on classification tasks. In addition to our primary findings, we conducted an analysis of the theoretical properties of loss functions used in classification tasks. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the role loss functions play in classification tasks and provides a foundation for further research on the subject. The research also indicates that the dominant mode of star formation shifts from the disk to the bulge as galaxies grow in mass, which is supported by theoretical models of galaxy evolution. The results provide valuable insights into the growth and evolution of bulges and the structure of galaxies, offering a new perspective on the role of bulges in shaping the mass-star formation rate relation.
